citation.author: Moser, Heather Rose
citation.title: 'A Crash of Worlds': How Red Dead Redemption II Creates a World Where Players Experience Empathy Through Character Performance
citation.type: MA thesis (Brigham Young University, Department of Theatre and Media Arts; ProQuest 29222749; BYU ScholarsArchive 9444)

discipline: theatre/media arts; performance studies; phenomenology; game studies
thesis: Open-world RPGs, and Red Dead Redemption II in particular, cultivate player empathy through character attachment, duration of play, and identification in a safe experimental space; the player is a performer (actor) who embodies Arthur Morgan, and the empathy practiced on this virtual 'other' becomes a bridge toward empathy for real, different people.
sections: Phenomenology and Ludology > The Experience of Play
Players as Performers > Research for the Role
Players as Performers > Differing Approaches and Emotional Connection to the Character
Developing Empathy > Embodying Character and Experience
Developing Empathy > Living Vicariously Through the Character
Developing Empathy > Empathizing With the Other
concepts: intersubjectivity / collision and overlap of lifeworlds
immersion phases (engagement, engrossment, total immersion; imaginative immersion)
moral intuition / justified vs. unjustified virtual violence
readings: Narrative open-world RPGs differ in kind from non-narrative genres (sports/FPS/battle royale), which may dampen rather than build empathy; the empathy claim is scoped to character-driven simulation games.
RDR2's spatial restrictions (clouded map, rock walls, instant death west of Blackwater, the 'invisible sniper') are necessary narrative scaffolding, not failures of openness.
The player occupies a triple position simultaneously: performer, character, and audience; a special empathy connection links all three at once.

First-time players resemble spectators discovering the story live, yielding a more 'sincere' performance; replayers align with the trained actor who knows the end from the beginning (Othello analogy).
Guilt over fictional characters' fates is nearly unique to games because the player chooses what happens (Jenkins).
The honor system carries an implicit ideology: without a mandated honor goal it still tacitly rewards the notion that good returns to those who put good out in the world.
Player and character share a doubled lifeworld structure (full overlap), unlike ordinary intersubjective contact where worlds only partially meet.

game_elements.how_treated: Central; Arthur (Dutch's lieutenant/surrogate son in the Van der Linde gang) moves toward recognizing guilt and resolving to do better; the arc bends with player honorable/dishonorable portrayal.

game_elements.element: The Downes encounter and tuberculosis infection
game_elements.how_treated: Read as the rigid, choice-free hinge: as Strauss's debt collector Arthur is forced to beat farmer Mr. Downes, who coughs blood (TB) on him; Arthur's advancing TB and impending death drive the mortality/morality reckoning that fuels the arc.

Extensively analyzed as RDR2's distinctive empathy-relevant mechanic: red-to-white gradient bar with tracking cowboy; skull-faced red vs. white-cowboy icons with sounds; consequences include store discounts/price hikes, NPC friendliness, honor-gated items (ebony revolver grip at a dishonor threshold), altered dialogue/cutscenes and vision-dreams.
game_elements.locus: Game Mechanics; The Experience of Play; Living Vicariously

game_elements.element: Four endings and spirit-animal visions (coyote / stag)
game_elements.how_treated: Endgame: Micah revealed as Pinkerton mole, Dutch beyond reason, shootout; choice to help John or grab loot. Dishonorable -> Micah kills Arthur, coyote (lightning storm) vision; honorable -> Arthur dies of TB, stag (sun rays) vision. The animals signal that player action shaped the kind of man Arthur became even though the basic plot is fixed.

After Arthur's death players control John; the grave differs by honor: high-honor adorned with flowers ('Hunger and Thirst for Righteousness'), low-honor bare ('Mourn for They Will Be Comforted'). Cited via Metz/TheGamer.

game_elements.element: Saint Denis 'pet' shack (implied rape) and reload-to-undo
game_elements.how_treated: Optional event from exploring an unvisited building outside Saint Denis: a 'friendly' man knocks Arthur out; black screen, belt unbuckling, 'pet'; Arthur wakes with drained vitals. Used to mark player/character lifeworld asymmetry: the player can reload a save to erase it for Arthur, but the player's own lifeworld still remembers.
Near Arthur's end the horse is shot and killed; touchstone for genuine grief over a virtual loss ('that horse was also theirs'), illustrating user-character empathy and attachment stakes.
Opening hideout teaches movement, shooting, hunting, fistfighting, riding, scavenging, weapon/item wheel, satchel; framed as the actor handed techniques/tools, with deliberately thin early backstory.

game_elements.element: Magic-'if' experiments (Valentine store robbery; countryside snakebite rescue)
game_elements.how_treated: Concrete paidia testing: robbing the Valentine general store with escalating bounty/lawmen; snakebite rescue (do nothing/he dies vs. give cure or suck out venom, earning honor and a free gun from the grateful man).

game_elements.element: Morally weighted incidents (KKK meeting; prisoner-coach rescue)
game_elements.how_treated: KKK members can be killed honor-neutral; killing the two officers in the prisoner-coach rescue earns dishonor while freeing the innocent prisoner restores some honor; illustrates Hartmann et al.'s justified/unjustified violence and guilt.

Fog-of-war revealed by travel with Arthur's hunting notes; yellow main-mission markers and white side-quest dots (some time-gated); impassable rock walls; 'wanted dead or alive' red zone east of Blackwater; instant death crossing the river west of Blackwater (the designers' 'invisible sniper').

Optional NPC conversations and the readable journal are empathy-builders that let players 'listen' to the other and access Arthur's private self (singing/whistling, hunting alone)—the condition the actor most desires.
game_elements.locus: Empathizing With the Other; Differing Approaches

themes: storytelling as the engine of empathy and social/cultural change
performance/acting as a model of ethical and emotional participation
the safe experimental space / ethical testing ground
responsibility, care-labor, and guilt as evidence of attachment
real-world transfer of empathy and its limits
reflexive call to industry to design empathy-encouraging systems
interlocutors: Melissa Lewis, Rene Weber and Nicholas Bowman

debate_axis_positions.position: Firmly performer; imports Stanislavskian acting theory to recast play as embodied performance of Arthur.
Strongly affirmative (games as empathy generators), conceding limits; positioned in the prosocial camp against the violence-effects tradition (Anderson et al.).
Experiential/first-person (lifeworld, immersion, felt emotion), contrasting with ideology-critique approaches.
Reads the honor system as tacit moral pedagogy ('implicit ideology'); descriptive rather than critical, aligned with the morality-focused strand (Hoffmann, Hartmann, Jenkins).

tensions: The central in-game-to-real-world empathy-transfer claim rests on theory and analogy, not the quantitative data the conclusion admits is missing.
Player race/gender effects on performing Arthur are explicitly bracketed despite the project being about empathy across difference.
The performer/agency frame frictions with forced/predetermined beats (Downes beating, fixed spine, four pre-authored endings).
The save-reload 'undo' both enables the safe-space thesis and undercuts the consequence/responsibility logic on which felt empathy depends (Saint Denis case).
Single-player, single-game scope; online/multiplayer and cross-game generalization deferred to future work.
